_work.title: Bulugh al-Watar fi Usul Ilm al-Athar — Geomancy Treatise (Princeton, Garrett)
_work.blurb: A manuscript treatise on geomancy (ilm al-raml) held at Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection), 20 leaves (40 pages). The title Bulugh al-Watar fi Usul Ilm al-Athar (Attaining the Desire in the Principles of the Science of Traces/Marks) refers to geomancy, which in Arabic is literally the 'science of the trace' — marks left in sand or earth by the diviner's stylus. The treatise comprises an introduction, five chapters (abwab) and a conclusion, discussing the 16 geomantic figures (al-ashkal), their names, properties, and the system of the geomantic house-chart (bayt). The text integrates the geomantic figures with humoral and planetary properties, and contains inline geomantic figure notations (the distinctive 1-or-2-dot-per-row patterns) embedded within the text columns. This compact treatise represents the concise, practical wing of the Arabic geomancy literature — focused on the operational system rather than philosophical elaboration.
_work.rights: Public Domain — manuscript (date unknown). Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
_work.creator: Anonymous

entries.title: Inline Geomantic Figure Notations (Raml Dot Patterns) — Bulugh al-Watar (p. 16)
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A page from Bulugh al-Watar (Princeton), a geomancy treatise, showing inline geomantic figure notations embedded within the Arabic text. At the bottom of the text block, small geomantic figures are written in the standard Arabic notation: each figure is a vertical stack of 4 rows, each row containing either one point (odd) or two points (even), representing a binary code of 4 bits (24 = 16 possible figures). Above each figure group are letter-labels (Arabic letters indicating which figure it is). These inline notations appear throughout Arabic geomancy manuals as both reference marks and worked examples — showing the reader exactly what each figure looks like in the binary dot notation used in practice. In Arabic geomancy, the 16 figures are generated by randomly marking rows in sand, then counting the points: an odd number of marks per row produces one point; even produces two. This page shows the notation system in its most compact, textual-integration mode.
